A.reason: Notes there is no project-level mapping or traceable basis for classifying projects into the two approaches, and that projects mix both approaches.
Questions per-coder saturation at 10–11 interviews while theoretical sampling continued into non-food projects; also flags the missing guide.
Identifies the missing interview guide or questions and how it may have shaped the chronological four-phase structure.
'Proven effective', 'growing interest' and robustness claims exceed staff self-report data; Limitations concede usability and impact were not examined.
Challenges generalisation from a narrow agri-food/bioeconomy sample and the unsupported 'did not diverge' claim to broader EU R&I.

B.reason: No project classification or per-project evidence for the typology or its prevalence claims.
Argues the dichotomy is undermined by admitted mixing and may be an ideal type that should be framed as such.
Questions saturation at 10–11 of 22 interviews alongside the claimed theoretical sampling.
The robustness and structural-causation claims are not supported, since usability and impact were not examined, as Limitations concede.
Sample scope and the unsupported non-divergence claim limit generalisation to wider European R&I.

C.reason: Prevalence claims cannot be traced because no project is assigned to either approach.
Tool robustness was never measured, and the Figure 1 transition model is not empirically grounded.
Causal wording about structural and project influence exceeds cross-sectional staff accounts; alternative explanations are not considered.
Distinguishes staff-only accounts from the actual experiences of citizens and marginalised groups.
No codebook or code list is provided, so the coding is not auditable; respects the limits on external resources.
